import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components'

A Spring Boot app signs users in through the [OpenID Provider](/build/openid-provider) with
[`oauth2Login`](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/reference/web/spring-security.html). Spring reads
discovery from `issuer-uri`.

<Aside type="note" title="What this was tested against">
  Spring Boot 4.1.2, Spring Security 7.1.2 and Java 21, on servlet (Spring MVC), against released
  `seamless-auth-api` v0.22.0 and `seamless-auth-oidc-provider` v0.3.0, on 2026-11-04. Nothing here
  needs API v0.23.0. See [What was and was not tested](#what-was-and-was-not-tested): this is a local
  test, not production verification.
</Aside>

---

## 1. Register The Client

`POST /admin/applications`:

```json
{
  "name": "Spring app",
  "clientType": "confidential",
  "firstParty": true,
  "tokenEndpointAuthMethod": "client_secret_basic",
  "redirectUris": ["http://127.0.0.1:13002/login/oauth2/code/seamless"],
  "postLogoutRedirectUris": ["http://127.0.0.1:13002/"],
  "grantTypes": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"]
}
```

Spring's default redirect is `{baseUrl}/login/oauth2/code/{registrationId}`. A shared secret needs
[`allow_client_secrets`](/build/openid-provider-connect-an-app#register-the-client). To avoid one, see
[Use `private_key_jwt`](#use-private_key_jwt).

---

## 2. Add The Dependencies

```xml
<parent>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version>4.1.2</version>
</parent>

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webmvc</artifactId>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-client</artifactId>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

---

## 3. Configure It

`application.yaml`:

```yaml
server:
  port: 13002
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      client:
        registration:
          seamless:
            client-id: ${SEAMLESS_CLIENT_ID}
            client-secret: ${SEAMLESS_CLIENT_SECRET}
            client-authentication-method: client_secret_basic
            authorization-grant-type: authorization_code
            scope: openid,email
        provider:
          seamless:
            issuer-uri: ${SEAMLESS_ISSUER}
```

**PKCE needs no setting in this version.** With the configuration above, Spring Security 7.1.2 sent
PKCE from a confidential client, which the provider requires. The Spring documentation covers this under
[`requireProofKey`](https://docs.spring.io/spring-security/reference/servlet/oauth2/client/authorization-grants.html).
Do not set it to `false`. Older versions were not tested. If yours does not send PKCE, the provider
answers `Authorization Server policy requires PKCE`.

Sign-out, so that it also ends the Seamless session, uses Spring's
[RP-initiated logout handler](https://docs.spring.io/spring-security/reference/servlet/oauth2/login/logout.html):

```java
@Configuration
public class SecurityConfig {
  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain security(HttpSecurity http, ClientRegistrationRepository registrations)
      throws Exception {
    var logout = new OidcClientInitiatedLogoutSuccessHandler(registrations);
    logout.setPostLogoutRedirectUri("{baseUrl}/");
    return http
        .authorizeHttpRequests((a) -> a.anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2Login(Customizer.withDefaults())
        .logout((l) -> l.logoutSuccessHandler(logout))
        .build();
  }
}
```

Read the user from `OidcUser`:

```java
@GetMapping("/")
String home(@AuthenticationPrincipal OidcUser user) {
  return "Signed in as " + user.getEmail() + ", subject " + user.getSubject() + ", acr "
      + user.getClaimAsString("acr");
}
```

The provider issues no `name` or `preferred_username` claim, so identify users by `getSubject()` or
`getEmail()`. Add the `seamless` scope for the `roles`
claim. Mapping `roles` to Spring authorities was not tested.

### Use `private_key_jwt`

Register the client with `"tokenEndpointAuthMethod": "private_key_jwt"` and your public `jwks`, as in
the [generic guide](/build/openid-provider-connect-an-app#register-the-client). Then set the method and
leave the secret empty:

```yaml
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      client:
        registration:
          seamless:
            client-secret: ''
            client-authentication-method: private_key_jwt
```

Add a token client that signs the assertion, following
[JWT Bearer client authentication](https://docs.spring.io/spring-security/reference/servlet/oauth2/client/client-authentication.html).
`oauth2Login` picks this bean up:

```java
@Bean
OAuth2AccessTokenResponseClient<OAuth2AuthorizationCodeGrantRequest> tokenClient()
    throws Exception {
  JWK key = JWK.parse(Files.readString(Path.of(System.getenv("SEAMLESS_PRIVATE_JWK_FILE"))));
  var client = new RestClientAuthorizationCodeTokenResponseClient();
  client.addParametersConverter(
      new NimbusJwtClientAuthenticationParametersConverter<>((registration) -> key));
  return client;
}
```

The file holds the private JWK with its `kid`, which must match the registered key.

---

## 4. Trust A Private CA

A publicly trusted certificate needs none of this. For a private CA, copy the JVM's trust store, import
your CA, and point the JVM at the copy, so the public CAs stay trusted:

```bash
cp "$JAVA_HOME/lib/security/cacerts" /tmp/truststore.jks
keytool -importcert -noprompt -alias seamless-local -file /ca.crt \
  -keystore /tmp/truststore.jks -storepass changeit
export JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=/tmp/truststore.jks -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword=changeit"
java -jar target/demo-0.0.1.jar
```

This covered discovery, the token call and the JWKS. `changeit` is the JDK's default store password.
Use your own for anything longer lived than a test.

The test ran this in a `maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21` container on the recipe's compose network, with
`SEAMLESS_ISSUER`, `SEAMLESS_CLIENT_ID` and `SEAMLESS_CLIENT_SECRET` set.

---

## 5. Check It

1. Open `http://127.0.0.1:13002/`. Every route needs a user, so the browser goes to the hosted page
   without an intermediate login page.
2. Sign in. A first-party client shows no consent page.
3. The page shows the user's email and `sub`. `acr` is `null` after a first email-code sign-up and was
   `phrh` after a passkey sign-in on the virtual authenticator.
4. Open `/logout` and confirm. The hosted page asks whether to sign out of everything or only this app.
   After **Sign out** the browser returns to `/`, which needs a user again, so it lands on the hosted
   sign-in page.

---

## Troubleshooting

Each of these was hit while testing.

| What you see                                                                                                  | Cause and fix                                                                                                                                                            |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| The app exits at startup: `Unable to resolve Configuration with the provided Issuer of "https://..."`         | Spring fetches discovery at startup. In the test the cause was the JVM not trusting the CA. See [step 4](#4-trust-a-private-ca). |

Registration and shared-secret errors are in the
[generic guide](/build/openid-provider-connect-an-app#troubleshooting).

---

## What Was And Was Not Tested

**Tested.** The configuration above, with both `client_secret_basic` and `private_key_jwt`, with
Playwright's Chromium and a virtual WebAuthn authenticator: a new user registering and a passkey sign-in
from a clean browser, ending on a page showing the user. Sign-out was run with `client_secret_basic`.
The stack was the local recipe from
[seamless-auth-oidc-provider#60](https://github.com/fells-code/seamless-auth-oidc-provider/pull/60)
(not merged at the time of writing), adjusted as described in the
[generic guide](/build/openid-provider-connect-an-app#what-was-and-was-not-tested).

**Not tested.** A browser that trusts the CA normally, a real authenticator, a publicly trusted
certificate, a production deployment, `https` or running behind a proxy (`server.forward-headers-strategy`),
WebFlux, mapping `roles` to authorities, refresh tokens, older Spring versions, or Spring as a resource
server.
